authors: Keddie, S.H., Baerenbold, O., Keogh, R.H. & Bradley, J.
title: Estimating sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic tests using latent class models that account for conditional dependence between tests: a simulation study
relevance: Quantifies exactly what goes wrong when latent class models assume conditional independence but the sources are correlated: sensitivities of the CORRELATED tests are OVERESTIMATED (median bias +0.094), while prevalence and the specificities of the uncorrelated tests are underestimated. That is the failure mode our three sources invite - the model was trained on labels derived from the same imagery as the NDVI reference, so those two are the correlated pair, and a naive latent class fit would inflate precisely their apparent recall. It would tell us what we want to hear. Also gives the conditional-dependence model formulations that are the correct fix.

authors: Okkaoglu, Y., Welton, N.J. & Jones, H.E.
title: Detecting departures from the conditional independence assumption in diagnostic latent class models: a simulation study
relevance: Shows the standard diagnostics cannot rescue us: residual correlation plots and pairwise G2/chi-square identified the genuinely correlated pair only 10-12% of the time while falsely flagging an innocent pair 50-65% of the time, and detected overall lack of fit in only about two-thirds of cases. So we could neither assume independence safely nor reliably detect its violation. Combined with the fact that three sources and two classes leave a JUST-IDENTIFIED model with zero degrees of freedom - fittable but untestable - this is the paper that says a three-source latent class analysis on C-CAP, the NDVI reference and the model would be unfalsifiable. The implication is constructive: get a fourth, genuinely independent source.
